27.0.s.en: 1. Those in charge of the monthly service

27.0.0.en: 1 Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand. 2 Over the first course for the first month was Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 3 Of the children of Perez was the chief of all the captains of the host for the first month. 4 And over the course of the second month was Dodai an Ahohite, and of his course was Mikloth also the ruler: in his course likewise were twenty and four thousand. 5 The third captain of the host for the third month was Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, a chief priest: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 6 This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his course was Ammizabad his son. 7 The fourth captain for the fourth month was Asahel the brother of Joab, and Zebadiah his son after him: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 8 The fifth captain for the fifth month was Shamhuth the Izrahite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 9 The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 10 The seventh captain for the seventh month was Helez the Pelonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 11 The eighth captain for the eighth month was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 12 The ninth captain for the ninth month was Abiezer the Anetothite, of the Benjamites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 13 The tenth captain for the tenth month was Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 14 The eleventh captain for the eleventh month was Benaiah the Pirathonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 15 The twelfth captain for the twelfth month was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand.

27.0.1.en: Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand. [1]

27.0.2.en: Here we find an account of the organization of the divisions of the kingdom’s army. David himself was a man of war, and did great deeds with the sword, and brought down many armies into battle, and now he organizes them after God has given him rest from his enemies. He did not gather them all together, because that might cause hardship to them and to the state; yet he did not disband them or scatter them all, because that might leave the kingdom in danger, and the people might forget the art of war which they had learned. Therefore he planned to keep a permanent force, but not a standing army. 1. He kept 240,000 armed men continually, perhaps as one organized division in one place in the kingdom. This force was sufficient to preserve safety and peace for the people, and we as true Christians must learn spiritual warfare, because we have spiritual enemies and we must take care to stand always against them. 2. He changed them every month, and thus the total of the militia was 288,000, perhaps a fifth of the able men of the kingdom, and by distributing them into 12 divisions they were educated and trained in military matters, yet no one was obliged to serve more than one month in the year at his own expense, and surely this was within their ability, except in emergencies, when it was easy for them to be gathered together quickly. This is part of the wisdom of leaders, that while they provide security for the people, they plan for this to be done in an easy and effective way and, as far as possible, as less of a burden on the people. 3. Each division had a chief captain besides the captains of thousands and hundreds, and these twelve are mentioned among David’s mighty men in (2 Sam 23; 1 Chr 11).

27.0.3.en: “The chief fathers” or “the heads of the fathers’ houses” are individuals or households who rendered regular service to King David with the materials needed for establishing the temple.

27.0.4.en: “Twenty and four thousand”: Some see that the number thousand does not mean an arithmetical thousand, but is an expression used to mean a division or battalion of whatever number.

27.1.0.en: Over the first course for the first month was Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. [2]

27.2.0.en: Of the children of Perez was the chief of all the captains of the host for the first month. [3]

27.3.0.en: And over the course of the second month was Dodai an Ahohite, and of his course was Mikloth also the ruler:

27.3.1.en: in his course likewise were twenty and four thousand. [4]

27.3.2.en: Mikloth was with David [4], either to take his place in the time of his absence or incapacity or after his death.

27.4.0.en: The third captain of the host for the third month was Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, a chief priest: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. [5]

27.4.1.en: Benaiah is called here a chief priest [5], but since the word “kohen” means priest or leader, his title here could be chief captain.

27.5.0.en: This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his course was Ammizabad his son. [6]

27.5.1.en: Benaiah’s son was in his division [6], and Asahel’s son was after him [7]. From this it appears that the organization of the militia was established at the beginning of David’s reign, because Asahel was killed by Abner while David was reigning in Hebron, and he renewed this method after he had finished his wars and put military affairs in this position as a preparation for peace in the reign of Solomon; so when we think that we are safe as long as we are in the body, we must be ready for spiritual wars.

27.5.2.en: There was a common saying in the East that carried a meaning, which kings sent to their enemies, that it is not fitting for one who puts on arms to boast like one who has gone to the battle and returned victorious. He must conquer and achieve victory, and then he may boast of his victory. A man ought not to boast beforehand of what will happen, for he knows not what a day may bring forth (Prov 27:1). Let him wait until the battle is finished, for “Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off” (1 Kgs 20:11). The Apostle says: “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor 10:12).

27.5.3.en: v Our standing here is not a safe standing. No, not until we are delivered from the currents of this present life and sail to the quiet harbor. Do not then be puffed up that you stand, but take heed lest you fall; for if Paul feared this, and he was more steadfast than all of us, how much more is it fitting for us to be on our guard?! [1]

27.5.4.en: v He who reviles others falls at once into the same sins. Therefore the blessed Paul counsels us: “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” [2].

27.5.5.en: v The first feature of the organization of military forces (military tactics) is to know how to stand well. Many things depend on this. Therefore he often speaks of standing firm, saying: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith” (1 Cor 16:13). And also: “stand fast... in the Lord” (Phil 4:1), and also: “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” And also: “and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13). Without doubt he does not mean just any way of standing, but the right way, and as many who have experience in wars know the utmost importance of knowing how to stand. If in the case of boxers and wrestlers the trainers mention this matter before everything, I mean standing firm, how much more must it have priority in wars and military affairs [3].

27.15.s.en: 2. The heads of the tribes of Israel

27.15.0.en: 16 Furthermore over the tribes of Israel: the ruler of the Reubenites was Eliezer the son of Zichri: of the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maachah: 17 Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok: 18 Of Judah, Elihu, one of the brethren of David: of Issachar, Omri the son of Michael: 19 Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel: 20 Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah: 21 Of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah: of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner: 22 Of Dan, Azareel the son of Jeroham. These were the princes of the tribes of Israel. 23 But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens. 24 Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David.

27.15.1.en: Furthermore over the tribes of Israel: the ruler of the Reubenites was Eliezer the son of Zichri:

27.15.2.en: of the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maachah. [16]

27.15.3.en: They still kept the order that Moses had arranged long ago in the wilderness, that each tribe must have a leader or chief, and it probably continued either by election or by succession in the same family, and those mentioned here are those who were found when these events were recounted; for Elihu or Eliab, who was chief of Judah, was the eldest son of Jesse, who came from the line of Nahshon and Salmon, who were chiefs of the tribe in the days of Moses, and we suppose that their authority was now less than it was when each tribe acted on its own, for now all the tribes are subject not only to the king alone, but also to the chief of the tribe.

27.15.4.en: Our Christianity urges us to submit not only to the king as supreme, but also to governors sent by him (1 Pet 2:13-14) for the execution of justice.

27.15.5.en: The list of the tribes came arranged in a certain order.

27.15.6.en: First the sons of Leah in a suitable order: the Reubenites, the Simeonites, the Levites, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.

27.15.7.en: After that the sons of Rachel: Joseph represented by his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh; then Benjamin.

27.15.8.en: The sons of Bilhah: given not in chronological order: Naphtali and Dan.

27.15.9.en: The sons of Zilpah: Gad and Asher are not mentioned here.

27.15.10.en: The names of the heads of the tribes of Israel in the days of David indicate the existence of cooperation, ease and stability between the king and the heads of the old tribes, unlike what happened in the days of Solomon, when a kind of dispute was found that appeared clearly immediately after Solomon’s death.

27.16.0.en: Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok: [17]

27.17.0.en: Of Judah, Elihu, one of the brethren of David:

27.17.1.en: of Issachar, Omri the son of Michael: [18]

27.18.0.en: Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah:

27.18.1.en: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel: [19]

27.19.0.en: Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah:

27.19.1.en: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah: [20]

27.20.0.en: Of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah:

27.20.1.en: of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner: [21]

27.20.2.en: From the tribe of Benjamin the chief was Jaasiel the son of Abner, and although Abner was an enemy of David and opposed his ascending the throne, David did not oppose this promotion, but perhaps himself recommended him for this high post, and this teaches us to repay evil with good. A wonderful picture of the person of David, who practiced the commandment of the Gospel while under the Law!

27.20.3.en: v No one can love his enemies, or do good to those who hate him, or suffer for those who wrong him. But if he remembers the human nature common to them, he does not mind the sufferings they cause him, and the more cruel they are to him, the more he is gentle with them. A father grieves and is saddened over his deranged son all the more as the son’s madness and violence increase.

27.20.4.en: Paul diagnosed the disease that causes those fierce attacks against him, so his concern for them and his care for them as sick people increased.

27.20.5.en: We hear him addressing us with exceeding kindness and tenderness about those who scourged him five times (2 Cor 24:11), and stoned him and bound him and shed his blood and desired to cut him in pieces, and he says of them: “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 2:10). And he also pressed hard on those who wrong them, saying: “Be not highminded, but fear: for if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee” (Rom 20:11, 21). And when he saw the judgment falling upon them, he could do nothing but what he was able to do, which was that he wept and mourned for them without ceasing [4].

27.20.6.en: v When you are one with those who attack you and are mingled with them, you overcome them (by love and faith). And just as leaven hidden in dough does not perish, but rather changes the nature of the dough, so also in the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore do not be afraid when I tell you that tribulations are coming, for your light no one can extinguish, but it overcomes all men [5].

27.21.0.en: Of Dan, Azareel the son of Jeroham.

27.21.1.en: These were the princes of the tribes of Israel. [22]

27.22.0.en: But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens. [23]

27.22.1.en: When David ordered the numbering of the people, he forbade the numbering of those under twenty years of age, and he thought by this that he would remove suspicion about what he had done with regard to the promise that they would not be numbered; but this was a weak precaution, because it was never the custom to number those under twenty, for the promise concerning their number was about men of action.

27.23.0.en: Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David. [24]

27.23.1.en: The census was not completed, because the wrath of the Lord came before Joab finished it; perhaps David was ashamed of his sin, so he asked that the records of the census not be presented publicly.

27.23.2.en: David refused to use this census, since this census was counted as a corruption that came in the age of David.

27.23.3.en: The census that David took of the people out of pride of heart was not good; it was never completed and was not done accurately, and was not recorded as a true census. For Joab was weary of it and completed it only in part, and David was ashamed of it and wished it to be forgotten, because the punishment fell on Israel on account of it, and the good man, returning to himself, cannot find pleasure in what angers God, and cannot use anything he obtained through sin. David took the census in a moment of pride and unbelief, but now he did not take a census but relied on the promises of God.

27.23.4.en: David had 12 officers in charge of local affairs. And he had counsellors and close friends who gave him counsel.

27.24.0.en: 25 And over the king’s treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah: 26 And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub: 27 And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite: 28 And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baal-hanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash: 29 And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai: 30 Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite: 31 And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David’s.

27.24.1.en: The last section of this chapter refers to the king’s possessions and sources of income that were used in his administration of the kingdom, and these multiplied during his reign. It is noticeable that in (Ezek 46:16-18), after more than four centuries, the possessions of the royal family were firmly defined.

27.24.2.en: David did not demand taxes from the people, and his hand did not extend to the spoils of war, for he left the latter for the account of the temple (1 Chr 26:26).

27.24.3.en: And over the king’s treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel:

27.24.4.en: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah: [25]

27.28.0.en: And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite:

27.28.1.en: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai: [29]

27.29.0.en: Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite:

27.29.1.en: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite: [30]

27.30.0.en: And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite.

27.30.1.en: All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David’s. [31]

27.30.2.en: The rulers of the king’s substance, as they were called, were concerned with supervising the king’s husbandry: his vineyards, his olive trees, his herds, his camels, his asses, and his flocks. Here there are no state ministers or sports officials or masters of ceremonies, but all are in a service suited to the simplicity of those days. David was a severe soldier, and a great teacher, and a great ruler, but he was a faithful steward over his possessions. So he took much under his hand and stored it, not for pleasure but for profit, for the king himself is served by the field (Eccl 5:9). Rulers who want their subjects to be diligent must give themselves as an example in diligence and in managing affairs. But we find that afterward they made the poor of the land vinedressers and husbandmen (2 Kgs 25:12), and now David entrusted these works to his great men.

27.31.0.en: 32 Also Jonathan David’s uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons: 33 And Ahithophel was the king’s counsellor: and Hushai the Archite was the king’s companion: 34 And after Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar: and the general of the king’s army was Joab.

27.31.1.en: Also Jonathan David’s uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe:

27.31.2.en: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons: [32]

27.31.3.en: Holy Scripture does not indicate anywhere the existence of an uncle of David serving as his counsellor, therefore some translate the word “uncle” as “the beloved.”

27.31.4.en: Those who supervised the king’s household were known for wisdom and the art of speech. His uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe, not only an expert in politics, but learned in the Holy Scriptures, and David made him his counsellor, and another, without doubt distinguished in learning and seasoned, he made the tutor of his sons, and Ahithophel, a cunning man, was also a counsellor to David, but faithful Hushai was his friend and the keeper of his secrets. It seems that he did not have many counsellors, but those he had were marked by great abilities. The wisdom of leaders appears in the choice of their servants, and David, in spite of the trusted ones and relatives beloved to him and the counsellors around him, preferred the word of God above all (Ps 119:24): “Thy testimonies also are my delight and my counsellors.”

27.32.0.en: And Ahithophel was the king’s counsellor: and Hushai the Archite was the king’s companion: [33]

27.32.1.en: Hushai was faithful; he saved David’s life from the counsel of Ahithophel (2 Sam 15-23).

27.33.0.en: And after Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar:

27.33.1.en: and the general of the king’s army was Joab. [34]

27.33.2.en: As an example, Ahithophel and his painful story recorded in (2 Sam 15; 17). He was like Joab, a man of great distinction, but not faithful.

27.33.3.en: Grant me a life of constant readiness

27.33.4.en: v My God, my soul blesses You always, for You have set me as a soldier in the army of salvation.

27.33.5.en: You are my commander, and You are my weapon; You are the giver of victory and the bestower of the crown.

27.33.6.en: You granted me to rise from my fall, and made me steadfast in You.

27.33.7.en: Let me cleave to You always, that I may not fall!

27.33.8.en: Accompany me all the way until I meet You face to face.

27.33.9.en: v In You I enjoy faith and love.

27.33.10.en: By faith I do not fear the enemy, the devil.

27.33.11.en: With You the powers of darkness have no strength against me, for You are with me.

27.33.12.en: And I do not fear death, for You are my life.

27.33.13.en: By love I challenge my weak nature.

27.33.14.en: I long for the salvation of all who oppose me.

27.33.15.en: I love all the sons of men, and I rejoice in their fellowship with You.

27.33.16.en: v Glory to You, O Lord of hosts, who keep Your children from evil!
